slides.heading: Earth as a system
slides.body_md: Part 1: the five spheres, energy from the Sun, and why places and seasons differ.

visual.alt: Flow chart from the Sun’s energy to the five spheres, to heating that differs by latitude, and to the seasons

slides.narration: The Earth is not just rock, water and air sitting side by side. They work together as one system, powered by energy from the Sun. In this part we meet the five spheres of the Earth, learn what happens to sunlight when it arrives, and find out why the poles are cold, the equator is hot, and why we have seasons.

slides.heading: Five spheres, one system
slides.body_md: The Earth system has five parts: the **atmosphere** (air), **hydrosphere** (liquid water), **cryosphere** (ice), **geosphere** (rock and soil) and **biosphere** (life). They constantly exchange matter and energy, and the Sun drives most of the exchanges.

visual.caption: The five spheres and how they interact: schematic.

slides.narration: The Earth system has five parts, called spheres. The atmosphere is the air, the hydrosphere is liquid water, the cryosphere is ice and snow, the geosphere is rock and soil, and the biosphere is all living things. None of them stands alone. They keep exchanging matter and energy, and energy from the Sun drives most of these exchanges. The arrows in the picture work both ways.

slides.heading: What is in each sphere?
slides.body_md: Many places belong to more than one sphere. Groundwater is **hydrosphere**, the soil that holds it is **geosphere**, and the roots and earthworms in it are **biosphere**.

rows: Liquid water on and under the ground
Rock, soil and the Earth’s interior
All living things and where they live

visual.alt: Table of the five spheres, what each contains and an example

slides.narration: This table lists what each sphere holds. Clouds and wind belong to the atmosphere. Oceans, rivers and groundwater belong to the hydrosphere. Glaciers and sea ice belong to the cryosphere. Mountains, volcanoes and soil belong to the geosphere. Forests, coral reefs and farms belong to the biosphere. Many places overlap. Soil is geosphere, but the roots and earthworms in it are the biosphere.

slides.heading: Worked example: the journey of a monsoon raindrop
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Trace a raindrop of the monsoon from the sea to a rice field, and name the spheres involved.

**Step 1.** The Sun heats the sea. Water leaves the **hydrosphere** and enters the **atmosphere** as vapour.

**Step 2.** The land is hotter than the sea, so moist air flows inland, rises, cools and forms clouds.

**Step 3.** Rain falls on a hill, runs into a stream and soaks the soil, which links the atmosphere, hydrosphere and **geosphere**.

**Step 4.** The rice crop, part of the **biosphere**, takes up the water.

rows: The Sun heats the Arabian Sea and water evaporates
Moist air flows to the hot land, rises, cools and forms clouds
Rain falls on a hill and runs into a stream
A farmer’s rice crop uses the water

visual.alt: Table that traces a monsoon raindrop through four steps and the spheres involved

slides.narration: Let us follow a raindrop. First the Sun heats the sea, and water evaporates into the air. The land heats faster than the sea, so moist air flows inland, rises and cools into clouds. Rain falls on a hill, runs into a stream and soaks the soil. At the end, a rice crop in a farmer field takes up the water. In this one journey four of the five spheres were involved.

slides.heading: When a volcano erupts
slides.body_md: One event can touch every sphere. A volcano begins in the **geosphere**, but its ash and gas enter the **atmosphere**, its heat can melt the **cryosphere**, and its ash falls on the **biosphere**.

rows: Lava and ash leave the Earth’s interior
New rock forms; land is covered
Ash and gas rise into the sky
Haze that can cool the weather for a time
Ice melts and a flood may follow
Ash falls on forests and fields
Plants may be buried; soil later gains minerals

visual.alt: Table showing how one volcanic eruption affects four spheres

slides.narration: A volcanic eruption shows how connected the spheres are. Lava and ash come from the geosphere. Ash and gas rise into the atmosphere, and a haze can cool the weather for a time. Hot lava that reaches a glacier melts ice in the cryosphere. Ash falling on forests and fields can bury plants in the biosphere, though later the soil may gain minerals.

slides.heading: Sunlight is radiation
slides.body_md: Energy from the Sun reaches us as **electromagnetic radiation**, which can travel through empty space. Sunlight contains **infrared** (felt as heat), **visible light** and **ultraviolet** (UV). The shares given here are approximate.

rows: Can burn skin; most is stopped by the ozone layer
Lets us see; used in photosynthesis

visual.alt: Table of ultraviolet, visible and infrared radiation with wavelength, approximate share of sunlight and main effect

slides.narration: Energy from the Sun travels through empty space as electromagnetic radiation. Sunlight has three main parts. Infrared radiation is about half of it, and we feel it as heat. Visible light is about forty percent, and it lets us see and helps plants make food. Ultraviolet radiation is under ten percent, and it can burn skin. These shares are approximate. Most ultraviolet is stopped by the ozone layer.

slides.heading: What happens to sunlight on Earth?
slides.body_md: About **30 percent** of the sunlight is reflected back to space by clouds, ice and the surface (approximate). The rest, about **70 percent**, is absorbed by the air, land and sea, which warm up and then give out infrared radiation.

visual.alt: Flow chart: sunlight is partly reflected and partly absorbed, the warm Earth gives out infrared radiation and greenhouse gases return some of it

slides.narration: When sunlight reaches the Earth, about thirty percent is reflected back to space by clouds, ice and bright surfaces. This is an approximate value. The other seventy percent or so is absorbed by the air, the land and the oceans. They warm up. Then the warm Earth gives out its own heat, as infrared radiation. Without this balance, the Earth would keep heating or cooling.

slides.heading: Light surfaces reflect, dark surfaces absorb
slides.body_md: How much a surface warms depends on how much light it **absorbs**. Fresh snow reflects most light and stays cold. A dark tar road absorbs most and gets hot.

visual.alt: Table of three surfaces, how much light each reflects and the result in sunshine

slides.narration: Different surfaces react differently to sunlight. Fresh snow reflects most of the light, so it stays cold. Green grass reflects some and warms a little. A black tar road reflects very little, so it absorbs most of the light and becomes very hot. That is why a white roof keeps a house cooler than a dark one.

slides.heading: The greenhouse effect
slides.body_md: The warm ground gives out **infrared radiation**. **Greenhouse gases** such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour absorb some of it and send part back down. This natural effect keeps the average surface temperature near **15 degrees Celsius**, instead of about minus 18 (approximate).

visual.alt: Flow chart of the greenhouse effect from sunlight warming the ground to a warmer surface

slides.narration: The ground warms in sunlight and gives out infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases in the air, such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour, absorb some of this heat and send part of it back down. This natural greenhouse effect is useful. It keeps the average temperature of the Earth near fifteen degrees Celsius. Without it, the average would be far below freezing.

slides.heading: Latitude: the same beam, a bigger patch
slides.body_md: At the equator at noon, sunlight falls almost straight down. At **60 degrees north** it falls at a slant, so the same beam spreads over **twice** the ground area, and each square metre is heated half as much. The patch length is $1 / \cos(\text{latitude})$ times the beam width.

slides.narration: Look at the picture. Two beams of sunlight have the same width. At the equator the beam falls straight down and covers a small patch of ground. At sixty degrees north it falls at a slant, and the same beam covers a patch twice as long. The energy is spread over twice the area, so each square metre is heated only half as much. This is one reason why the poles are colder than the equator.

slides.heading: Worked example: energy at 30 degrees north
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** At noon on an equinox day the equator receives 800 W m⁻² (given). Find the energy per square metre at 30° N.

**Step 1.** The area factor is $1 / \cos 30° = 1 / 0.866 = 1.15$, so the beam covers about 1.15 times the area.

**Step 2.** Energy per square metre $= 800 \times \cos 30° = 800 \times 0.866 = 692.8$.

**Step 3.** So about **693 W m⁻²** reaches each square metre, which is a little less than at the equator.

rows: 1 divided by cos 30° = 1 divided by 0.866 = about 1.15

visual.alt: Table with the area factor and energy per square metre at 30 degrees north

slides.narration: Let us work out the energy at thirty degrees north. The equator gets eight hundred watts on each square metre. At thirty degrees north the same beam is spread over about one point one five times the area. So each square metre gets eight hundred times zero point eight six six, which is about six hundred and ninety three watts. That is a little less than at the equator.

slides.heading: Tilt of the axis and the seasons
slides.body_md: The Earth’s axis is tilted by about **23.5 degrees** and always points the same way as the Earth goes round the Sun. When the northern half leans towards the Sun (June), it has **summer**; when it leans away (December), **winter**. The distance to the Sun is **not** the cause.

slides.narration: The axis of the Earth is tilted by about twenty three and a half degrees. As the Earth goes round the Sun, the axis keeps pointing the same way. In June the northern half leans towards the Sun, so sunlight is more direct and the days are longer. That is summer in the north. Six months later it leans away, and it is winter. The Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, so distance is not the cause.

slides.narration: Energy flows through the Earth system, but matter goes round and round. The same carbon, nitrogen and water are used again and again. In this part we follow these three cycles, and then see how burning fuels, cutting forests and using fertiliser disturb them. We end with what each of us can do.

slides.heading: Energy flows, matter cycles
slides.body_md: Sunlight arrives, does its work and leaves as heat. Matter has nowhere else to go, so it **cycles** between air, water, rock and living things.

rows: Flows through and leaves as heat
Goes round and round in cycles

slides.narration: Energy and matter behave differently on Earth. Energy comes from the Sun, flows through the system and leaves as heat. Matter does not arrive from outside in large amounts. Carbon, nitrogen and water therefore go round in cycles, passing between air, water, rock and living things, and they are used over and over again.

slides.heading: The carbon cycle
slides.body_md: Plants and algae take **carbon dioxide** from the air by photosynthesis. Animals eat plants. Respiration and decomposition return carbon dioxide to the air. Some remains become **fossil fuels**, and burning them releases carbon dioxide. The ocean takes in and gives out carbon dioxide.

slides.heading: Fixation, nitrification, denitrification
slides.body_md: **Fixation** changes nitrogen gas into usable compounds. **Nitrification** changes ammonia into nitrates. **Denitrification** changes nitrates back into nitrogen gas. Pulse crops such as gram and moong host *Rhizobium* in their root nodules.

slides.narration: Three processes are important. In nitrogen fixation, nitrogen gas is changed into compounds, by Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules of pulse plants, by lightning, and in fertiliser factories. In nitrification, soil bacteria change ammonia into nitrates. In denitrification, bacteria in waterlogged soil change nitrates back into nitrogen gas, which returns to the air.

slides.narration: The water cycle is driven by the heat of the Sun. Water evaporates from seas, and plants lose vapour through their leaves by transpiration. The vapour rises and cools, and condensation makes clouds. Rain or snow falls as precipitation. Water then flows over the land as runoff, or soaks into the ground. The cycle is never ending. About ninety seven percent of Earth water is in the oceans, which is an approximate value.

slides.heading: Worked example: evaporation from a tank
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A water tank has a surface area of 500 m². In a day its level falls 4 mm because of evaporation (given). How many litres evaporate?

**Step 1.** Convert the depth: 4 mm = 0.004 m.

**Step 2.** Volume = area × depth = 500 × 0.004 = **2 m³**.

**Step 3.** 1 m³ = 1000 litres, so the tank loses 2 × 1000 = **2000 litres**.

visual.alt: Table with the depth, volume and litres of water lost by evaporation from a tank

slides.narration: Let us find how much water a tank loses in a day. Change four millimetres to metres, which is zero point zero zero four. Multiply the area of five hundred square metres by this depth. That gives two cubic metres. One cubic metre is one thousand litres, so the tank loses two thousand litres of water in a day by evaporation.

slides.heading: Human impact on the carbon cycle and the climate
slides.body_md: Before the late 1800s the air held about **280 ppm** of carbon dioxide. As of the early 2020s it holds about **420 ppm** (approximate). The extra gas comes mostly from burning **fossil fuels** and from **deforestation**, and it strengthens the greenhouse effect.

visual.alt: Table of human activities, what each does and its effect on the cycles and the climate

slides.narration: People have changed the cycles. Before the late eighteen hundreds the air held about two hundred and eighty parts per million of carbon dioxide. As of the early twenty twenties it holds about four hundred and twenty, an approximate figure. The extra gas comes mostly from burning coal, oil and gas, and from cutting forests. Too much fertiliser and some farming practices add to the problems too.

slides.heading: Worked example: how much has carbon dioxide risen?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A gas rises from 300 ppm to 360 ppm (illustrative). Find the percentage rise.

**Step 1.** Rise = 360 − 300 = 60 ppm.

**Step 2.** Percentage rise = 60 / 300 × 100 = **20 %**.

**Step 3.** A rise of this kind in a greenhouse gas holds more heat near the surface.

visual.alt: Table with the rise and percentage rise in the concentration of a gas

slides.narration: Let us find a percentage rise. A gas goes from three hundred to three hundred and sixty parts per million. This is an illustrative case. The rise is sixty. Divide sixty by three hundred and multiply by one hundred. The answer is twenty percent. A rise like this in a greenhouse gas holds more heat near the surface.

slides.heading: Warming and its effects
slides.body_md: The Earth’s average temperature has risen by about **1.1 degrees Celsius** since the late 1800s (approximate, as of the early 2020s). Effects include melting ice, rising sea level and more extreme weather.

nodes.label: More heat held near the surface

visual.alt: Flow chart from more greenhouse gases to a higher temperature and then melting ice, rising sea and changing weather

slides.narration: More greenhouse gases hold more heat near the surface, so the average temperature rises. Since the late eighteen hundreds it has risen by about one point one degrees Celsius, which is approximate and given as of the early twenty twenties. The effects include melting glaciers and sea ice, a rising sea level and more extreme weather, such as heavy rain and heat waves.

slides.heading: Fertilisers and the nitrogen cycle
slides.body_md: Too much nitrogen fertiliser washes into ponds and rivers. The extra nitrates make **algae** grow too fast. When the algae die, decomposers use up the dissolved **oxygen**, and fish die.

visual.alt: Flow chart from fertiliser washing into a lake to algae growing, dying, decomposers using up oxygen and fish dying

slides.narration: Fertilisers add nitrogen compounds to the soil, which helps crops. But when farmers use too much, rain washes the extra into ponds and rivers. The nitrates make algae grow very fast. Later the algae die and rot, and decomposers use up the oxygen dissolved in the water. Without oxygen, the fish cannot breathe and they die.

sections.heading: 1. The Earth as interconnected spheres
sections.body_md:
The Earth works as one **system** made of five parts, called **spheres**: the **atmosphere** (air), the **hydrosphere** (liquid water), the **cryosphere** (frozen water), the **geosphere** (rock, soil and the interior) and the **biosphere** (all life). Matter and energy move between them all the time, and the Sun drives most of the movement.

One event usually touches several spheres. In the monsoon, heat from the Sun makes sea water evaporate (hydrosphere to atmosphere). Moist air flows over the hot land, rises and cools, and rain falls on hills and fields (atmosphere to geosphere and biosphere). A volcanic eruption begins in the geosphere, puts ash and gas in the atmosphere, can melt ice of the cryosphere and buries plants of the biosphere, and its haze can cool the weather for a time.

sections.heading: 2. Sunlight: radiation that warms the Earth
sections.body_md:
Sunlight is **electromagnetic radiation**, which travels through empty space. It has three main parts. **Infrared** (about half of the energy, approximate) is felt as heat. **Visible light** (about 40 percent, approximate) lets us see and powers photosynthesis. **Ultraviolet** (under 10 percent, approximate) can burn skin, and the ozone layer stops most of it.

At the top of the atmosphere a surface facing the Sun receives about **1361 W m⁻²** (approximate). About **30 percent** of the sunlight is **reflected** by clouds, ice and the surface (approximate). The rest, about 70 percent, is **absorbed** by the air, land and sea, which warm up and give out infrared radiation. Light surfaces such as fresh snow reflect more and stay cooler; dark surfaces such as tar absorb more and get hotter.

sections.heading: 3. The greenhouse effect, latitude and the seasons
sections.body_md:
The warm ground gives out infrared radiation. **Greenhouse gases** such as carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour absorb some of it and send part back down. This **greenhouse effect** keeps the average surface temperature near 15 °C instead of about −18 °C (approximate). The effect is natural and useful; trouble starts when extra gases strengthen it.

**Latitude.** At the equator the Sun is nearly overhead. At higher latitudes its rays slant, so a beam of the same width covers a larger patch of ground, of length $1/\cos(\text{latitude})$ times the width. At 60° the patch is twice as long, so each square metre receives about half the energy.

**Seasons.** The axis of the Earth is tilted by about **23.5 degrees** and points the same way all year. The hemisphere that leans towards the Sun gets more direct rays and longer days (summer). The other has winter. Distance from the Sun is not the cause: the Earth is nearest to the Sun in early January.

key_terms.definition_md: A gas such as carbon dioxide or methane that absorbs heat radiated by the ground.

sections.heading: 4. The carbon cycle
sections.body_md:
Carbon moves between the air, living things, the ocean and rocks. Plants and algae take in **carbon dioxide** by photosynthesis and build sugars and wood. Animals get carbon by eating. **Respiration** by all living things, and **decomposition** by bacteria and fungi, return carbon dioxide to the air. Some buried remains change over millions of years into **fossil fuels**: coal, oil and natural gas. Burning them, or burning wood, releases carbon dioxide at once. The ocean takes in and gives out the gas.

The air held about 280 ppm of carbon dioxide before the late 1800s and about 420 ppm as of the early 2020s (both approximate).

Coal, oil or natural gas, formed from ancient living things.
Parts per million: the number of molecules of a gas in a million molecules of air.

sections.heading: 5. The nitrogen and water cycles
sections.body_md:
**Nitrogen.** Air is about 78 percent nitrogen gas (approximate), but plants cannot take it up. **Nitrogen fixation** changes it into ammonia or nitrates: bacteria such as *Rhizobium* in the root nodules of pulses, lightning, and fertiliser factories do this. **Nitrification** is the change of ammonia to nitrates by soil bacteria. Plants absorb nitrates and make proteins, and animals eat the plants. **Decomposers** turn dead remains and wastes into ammonia. **Denitrification** by bacteria in waterlogged soil changes nitrates back to nitrogen gas.

**Water.** The Sun’s heat causes **evaporation** and plants lose vapour by **transpiration**. The vapour cools and **condenses** into clouds. **Precipitation** brings rain and snow. **Runoff** and **infiltration** return water to rivers, groundwater and the sea. About 97 percent of the water on Earth is in the oceans (approximate).

sections.heading: 6. Human impact on the cycles and the climate
sections.body_md:
Burning **fossil fuels** moves carbon that was stored for millions of years into the air within a short time. **Deforestation** releases the carbon stored in trees and leaves fewer trees to take carbon dioxide in. Rice fields and cattle give out **methane**. These add to the greenhouse gases, strengthen the greenhouse effect and raise the average temperature, by about 1.1 °C since the late 1800s (approximate, as of the early 2020s). Effects include melting ice, rising sea level and more extreme weather.

Too much nitrogen **fertiliser** washes into ponds and rivers and makes algae grow too much. When the algae die, decomposers use up the dissolved oxygen and fish die.

**What we can do:** use solar, wind and hydro power; plant and protect trees; use public transport, cycles or walking; use fertiliser only as needed and grow pulses; save energy and water.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying that distance from the Sun causes the seasons.
- Writing that the greenhouse effect is always harmful, or that carbon dioxide is the only greenhouse gas.
- Writing that plants absorb nitrogen gas directly.
- Mixing up nitrification (ammonia to nitrates) and denitrification (nitrates to nitrogen gas).
- Giving numbers such as 30 % reflected or 420 ppm without saying they are approximate, or without a date.
- Drawing a cycle without arrows showing direction.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a name, a sphere or one process.
- 2-mark items: two points or one cause and one effect.
- 3-mark items: three short correct points, often with an example.
- 5-mark items: a labelled diagram or flow, ordered steps and examples.

cards.front_md: Name the five spheres of the Earth system.
cards.back_md: Atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, geosphere and biosphere.

cards.front_md: What does the cryosphere contain?
cards.back_md: Frozen water: snow, glaciers, sea ice and lake ice.

cards.front_md: What is the biosphere?
cards.back_md: All living things and the places where life is found.

cards.front_md: Which sphere does groundwater belong to?
cards.back_md: The hydrosphere.

cards.front_md: Which spheres does a volcanic eruption link?
cards.back_md: It begins in the geosphere and affects the atmosphere, the cryosphere and the biosphere.

cards.front_md: Name one way the monsoon links two spheres.
cards.back_md: The Sun heats the sea, so water moves from the hydrosphere to the atmosphere and later falls as rain.

cards.front_md: What kind of energy is sunlight?
cards.back_md: Electromagnetic radiation, which can travel through empty space.

cards.front_md: Name the three main parts of sunlight.
cards.back_md: Infrared, visible light and ultraviolet radiation.

cards.front_md: Which part of sunlight is felt mainly as heat?
cards.back_md: Infrared radiation.

cards.front_md: What does the ozone layer do?
cards.back_md: It stops most of the ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.

cards.front_md: About how much sunlight is reflected back to space?
cards.back_md: About 30 percent (approximate).

cards.front_md: What happens to the sunlight that is not reflected?
cards.back_md: It is absorbed by the air, land and sea, which warm up and give out infrared radiation.

cards.front_md: Why does fresh snow stay cold in sunshine?
cards.back_md: It reflects most of the light, so it absorbs little energy.

cards.front_md: What is the greenhouse effect?
cards.back_md: Greenhouse gases absorb some of the heat radiated by the ground and send part back, keeping the surface warmer.

cards.front_md: Name three greenhouse gases.
cards.back_md: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour.

cards.front_md: Why are higher latitudes colder?
cards.back_md: Sunlight arrives at a slant, so the same energy spreads over a larger area.

cards.front_md: How much larger is the sunlit patch at 60 degrees latitude?
cards.back_md: About twice as long, because 1 divided by cos 60 degrees is 2.

cards.front_md: By how many degrees is the Earth’s axis tilted?
cards.back_md: About 23.5 degrees.

cards.front_md: What causes the seasons?
cards.back_md: The tilt of the axis, which changes how directly sunlight falls on each hemisphere. Not the distance from the Sun.

cards.front_md: Which hemisphere has summer in June?
cards.back_md: The Northern Hemisphere, because it leans towards the Sun.

cards.front_md: How do plants take carbon from the air?
cards.back_md: They take in carbon dioxide by photosynthesis and build sugars and wood.

cards.front_md: Name two processes that return carbon dioxide to the air.
cards.back_md: Respiration, decomposition and burning.

cards.front_md: How are fossil fuels formed?
cards.back_md: Buried remains of ancient living things change over millions of years into coal, oil and gas.

cards.front_md: What percentage of air is nitrogen gas?
cards.back_md: About 78 percent (approximate).

cards.front_md: What is nitrogen fixation?
cards.back_md: Changing nitrogen gas into compounds plants can use, by bacteria such as Rhizobium, lightning or factories.

cards.front_md: What is nitrification?
cards.back_md: The change of ammonia into nitrates by soil bacteria.

cards.front_md: What is denitrification?
cards.back_md: The change of nitrates back into nitrogen gas by bacteria in waterlogged soil.

cards.front_md: List the steps of the water cycle.
cards.back_md: Evaporation, transpiration, condensation, precipitation, runoff and infiltration.

cards.front_md: How much carbon dioxide was in the air as of the early 2020s?
cards.back_md: About 420 ppm, compared with about 280 ppm before the late 1800s (approximate).

cards.front_md: Name two human activities that raise carbon dioxide.
cards.back_md: Burning fossil fuels and cutting forests.

cards.front_md: Why is too much fertiliser harmful to a lake?
cards.back_md: Runoff makes algae grow too much; when they die, decomposers use up the oxygen and fish die.

cards.front_md: Give three actions that reduce human impact on the cycles and climate.
cards.back_md: Use solar or wind power, plant trees and use fertiliser carefully.

Heat from the Sun links the atmosphere, the hydrosphere and the geosphere, and the rain feeds the biosphere.

questions.solution_md: The Sun warms the land more than the sea, so the air above the land rises and moist air flows in from the sea. This links atmosphere, hydrosphere and geosphere, and the rain waters crops and forests — option (c).

**Reason (R):** The Sun’s heat makes water evaporate from the Arabian Sea.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. Evaporation supplies the water vapour, but the heavy rain on the slopes is mainly because moist air is forced up the hills, where it cools and condenses. So R does not explain A — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Heavy rain on a hillside in the Western Ghats washes soil into a stream. Name two spheres that interact here and state what each contributes.

answer.model_answer_md: The atmosphere interacts with the geosphere. The atmosphere supplies the rain, which is water falling from clouds. The geosphere supplies the loose soil, which the moving water carries away into the stream, a part of the hydrosphere.

questions.stem_md: A large volcanic eruption sends ash and sulfur gases into the air. Describe one effect on each of the atmosphere, the geosphere and the biosphere.

In the geosphere, lava and ash build new rock and cover the land. On the biosphere, ash can bury plants and animals nearby, although later it may enrich the soil with minerals.

questions.stem_md: Name the five spheres of the Earth and state what each contains. Using a monsoon season as an example, show how at least four of them interact.

answer.model_answer_md: The atmosphere is the air around the Earth. The hydrosphere is liquid water such as seas, rivers and groundwater. The geosphere is rock, soil and the interior. The cryosphere is snow and ice. The biosphere is all living things. In the monsoon, the Sun heats the land and sea, and water evaporates from the sea into the atmosphere. Moist air rises over land, cools and falls as rain. The rain fills rivers, soaks into the soil of the geosphere and helps crops and forests of the biosphere grow. Snow on mountains in the cryosphere later melts to feed rivers.

questions.passage_md:
After a big volcanic eruption, a weather station near the volcano records the average temperature of the region against a normal year. The readings below are illustrative (given).

| Days after eruption | Haze in the upper air | Temperature change (°C) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | None | 0.0 |
| 30 | Thick | −0.3 |
| 90 | Thick | −0.6 |
| 180 | Thin | −0.3 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) atmosphere, made of ash and gas from the geosphere

**(b)** It was coolest at 0.6 degrees below normal, after 90 days.

**(c)** (i) When the haze was thick, at 30 and 90 days, the temperature was lower. The haze reflected part of the sunlight, so less energy reached the ground. When the haze thinned at 180 days, the cooling became smaller.

**OR** (ii) The temperature will rise back towards normal. At 180 days the haze is thin and the cooling has already fallen from 0.6 to 0.3 degrees, so as the haze clears more sunlight will reach the ground.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Ash and gas from the Earth’s interior came from the geosphere and now hang in the air, so the haze is in the atmosphere — option (d).

**(b)** The lowest value in the table is −0.6 °C.

**(c)** (i) Thick haze, more cooling; thin haze, less cooling; less sunlight reaches the ground.

(ii) Temperature returns to normal as haze clears.

questions.stem_md: Which statement describes the natural greenhouse effect correctly?

options.text_md: A layer of glass in the sky stops sunlight from reaching the ground.
Some gases in the air absorb heat radiated by the ground and send part of it back, which keeps the surface warmer.
Heat from inside the Earth is the main source of warmth at the surface.
Greenhouse gases reflect all the sunlight back into space.

questions.solution_md: The ground warms and gives out infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb some of it and send part back down, so the surface is warmer than it would otherwise be — option (b).

questions.stem_md: On a winter morning in Shimla you stand in the sunshine and feel warmth on your face, although you cannot see the radiation that is mainly responsible. Which radiation is it?

options.text_md: Infrared radiation
Ultraviolet radiation
Visible light
Sound waves

questions.solution_md: Sunlight contains infrared, visible and ultraviolet radiation. Infrared is invisible and is felt mainly as heat — option (a). Sound waves are not part of sunlight.

questions.stem_md: On a sunny day a freshly snow-covered field stays much cooler than a black tar road next to it. The best explanation is that the snow:

options.text_md: reflects most of the sunlight, while the tar absorbs most of it
absorbs more sunlight than the tar
gives out heat of its own
is higher up and nearer to the Sun

questions.solution_md: Light-coloured surfaces such as fresh snow reflect most sunlight, so they absorb little energy. Dark tar absorbs most of it and gets hot — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A car parked in the sun with its windows shut becomes much hotter inside than outside. How is this like the greenhouse effect?

options.text_md: The glass makes new sunlight inside the car.
The engine heats the car even when it is off.
The glass reflects all the sunlight away from the seats.
Sunlight passes in through the glass, and the heat given out by the seats and dashboard is held in.

questions.solution_md: Sunlight enters through the glass and warms the objects inside. They give out infrared radiation, which cannot easily pass out, so the air inside heats up. Greenhouse gases act in a similar way — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A torch held straight above a table makes a small bright circle. Tilted, it makes a bigger, dimmer oval. What does this show about places near the poles?

options.text_md: The Sun is much farther from the poles.
Sunlight falls at a slant there, so the same energy is spread over a larger area.
There is no sunlight at the poles in any month.
Sunlight at the poles is a different kind of radiation.

questions.solution_md: Near the poles the Sun’s rays reach the ground at a low angle, like the tilted torch. The same energy covers a larger area, so each square metre is heated less — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Delhi has its hot summer around June, while Sydney is cool at that time. This is mainly because in June:

options.text_md: the Earth is at its nearest point to the Sun
the Sun gives out more energy in June
the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun because of the tilt of the Earth’s axis
the Earth stops rotating for some weeks

questions.solution_md: The axis of the Earth is tilted by about 23.5 degrees. In June the northern half leans towards the Sun, so it gets more direct sunlight and longer days. The southern half leans away — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The Earth is a little nearer to the Sun in early January, when it is winter in India. What does this tell us about the cause of the seasons?

options.text_md: Winter in India is caused by the Earth being closest to the Sun.
The Earth’s orbit is exactly a circle, so there are no seasons.
Seasons are caused by the Moon.
Distance from the Sun is not the main cause, and the tilt of the axis is.

questions.solution_md: If distance were the cause, January would be warm in India. It is cold, so the cause is the tilt of the axis, which changes how directly sunlight falls — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Without any greenhouse gases the average temperature at the Earth’s surface would be far below freezing (about −18 °C, approximate).

**Reason (R):** Greenhouse gases absorb part of the heat radiated by the ground and send some of it back.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. The returned heat is what raises the surface temperature to the present average of about 15 °C, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When it is summer in Australia it is winter in India.

**Reason (R):** In that month the whole Earth is nearer to the Sun.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true because the two hemispheres lean in opposite directions. R is false, because the distance is not the cause and the whole Earth cannot be near and far at once for two places — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Sunlight contains only visible light.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Sunlight also contains infrared radiation, which we feel as heat, and a small share of ultraviolet radiation.

questions.stem_md: Radiation with a wavelength just longer than that of red light is called ______ radiation.
questions.solution_md: Infrared lies beyond the red end of the visible spectrum.

questions.stem_md: Match each item (column I) with a statement about it (column II).

options.text_md: Ultraviolet
Visible light
Infrared
Greenhouse gas

questions.solution_md: Ultraviolet radiation can burn skin; visible light drives photosynthesis; infrared is felt as warmth; a greenhouse gas absorbs heat radiated by the ground.

questions.stem_md: Just above the atmosphere, sunlight delivers about 1361 W m⁻² to a surface facing the Sun (approximate). About 30 % of this sunlight is reflected back to space (approximate), and the rest is absorbed by the air, land and sea. Taking these values, find the power absorbed by each square metre of such a surface. Give the answer to the nearest whole number.
questions.solution_md: Fraction absorbed $= 1 - 0.3 = 0.7$. Power absorbed $= 1361 \times 0.7 = 952.7 \approx 953\ \text{W m}^{-2}$.

questions.stem_md: At noon on an equinox day, level ground at the equator receives about 900 W m⁻² of sunlight (given). questions.solution_md: Area is 2 times larger, so each square metre gets $\dfrac{1}{2}$ of the equator value. Sunlight per square metre $= \dfrac{900}{2} = 450\ \text{W m}^{-2}$.

questions.stem_md: Name the three kinds of radiation in sunlight that reach the Earth. State one effect of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Sunlight has infrared, visible and ultraviolet radiation. Infrared is felt as heat and warms the surface. Visible light lets us see and is used by plants for photosynthesis. Ultraviolet radiation can burn skin and kill germs in small amounts.

questions.solution_md: Infrared warms; visible light for sight and photosynthesis; ultraviolet burns skin.

questions.stem_md: Why is the weather at 60° N, such as in Norway, colder than at the equator, even on the same day with a clear sky?

answer.model_answer_md: At 60° N the Sun’s rays strike the ground at a slant, so the same beam of energy is spread over about twice the ground area compared with the equator. Each square metre therefore receives less energy and is heated less.

questions.solution_md: Slanting rays spread the energy over a larger area.

marking_scheme.step: Rays strike at a slant at higher latitude
The same energy spreads over a larger area, so less per square metre

questions.stem_md: Explain the greenhouse effect. Name two greenhouse gases and say why the effect is useful to life.

answer.model_answer_md: The ground absorbs sunlight and gives out heat as infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane absorb part of this heat and send some back towards the ground. This natural effect keeps the average temperature of the Earth near 15 degrees Celsius, so water stays liquid and life is possible.

questions.solution_md: Ground gives out infrared; gases absorb and return some; keeps Earth warm for life.

marking_scheme.step: Ground gives out heat as infrared radiation
Greenhouse gases absorb part and return it, two gases named
Keeps the Earth warm enough for liquid water and life

questions.stem_md: Explain, with the tilt of the Earth’s axis, why Delhi has a longer, warmer day in June than in December.

answer.model_answer_md: The axis of the Earth is tilted by about 23.5 degrees and always points the same way as the Earth goes round the Sun. In June the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun, so sunlight falls more directly and the days are longer. In December it leans away, so the sunlight is more slanting and the days are shorter.

questions.solution_md: Tilt; north leans towards Sun in June; more direct rays and longer days.

marking_scheme.step: Axis tilted by about 23.5 degrees, pointing the same way all year
In June the north leans towards the Sun: direct rays and longer days
In December it leans away: slanting rays and shorter days

questions.stem_md: Describe what happens to the sunlight that reaches the Earth, and explain how latitude and the tilt of the axis cause different amounts of heating and the seasons.

answer.model_answer_md: About 30 percent of the sunlight is reflected back to space by clouds, ice and the surface, and the rest is absorbed by the air, land and oceans, which warm up. The warm ground gives out infrared radiation, and greenhouse gases return part of it, which keeps the surface warm. Near the equator the rays are almost overhead, so energy is concentrated. Near the poles the rays are slanting, so the same energy spreads over a larger area. The tilt of 23.5 degrees makes each hemisphere lean towards the Sun for half the year, giving summer, and away for the rest, giving winter.

questions.solution_md: Reflected, absorbed, re-radiated; latitude spreads energy; tilt gives seasons.

marking_scheme.step: About 30 % reflected and the rest absorbed (approximate values)
Ground radiates infrared and greenhouse gases return part of it
Latitude: direct rays at the equator, slanting rays and larger area near the poles
Tilt of the axis gives summer when leaning towards the Sun and winter when leaning away

questions.stem_md: A banyan tree in a village has grown for fifty years and now weighs several tonnes. Most of the carbon in its wood came from:

options.text_md: carbon dioxide in the air, taken in by its leaves
minerals taken in from the soil
carbon in the water that it absorbed
oxygen gas taken in at night

questions.solution_md: Plants build sugars and wood from carbon dioxide of the air during photosynthesis. Soil minerals and water do not supply the carbon of wood — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The carbon stored in a lump of coal was once part of:

options.text_md: rocks that melted in a volcano
sea water that evaporated
gases that came from the Moon
plants that were buried and changed over millions of years

questions.solution_md: Coal formed from the remains of ancient plants that were buried and changed by heat and pressure over millions of years — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A farmer pulls up a gram plant and sees small swellings on its roots. Bacteria inside them change nitrogen gas of the air into compounds that the plant can use. This process is called:

options.text_md: nitrogen fixation
nitrification
denitrification
transpiration

questions.solution_md: Turning nitrogen gas into usable compounds is nitrogen fixation, done by bacteria such as Rhizobium in root nodules — option (a). Nitrification changes ammonia to nitrates, and denitrification returns nitrogen gas to the air.

questions.stem_md: Soil bacteria in a vegetable garden change ammonia from rotting leaves into nitrates, which the vegetable roots then absorb. This step is called:

options.text_md: denitrification
nitrogen fixation from the air
photosynthesis
nitrification

questions.solution_md: The change of ammonia to nitrates by soil bacteria is nitrification — option (d). Nitrogen fixation starts from nitrogen gas, and denitrification ends with nitrogen gas.

questions.stem_md: Air is about 78 % nitrogen (approximate), yet a wheat plant without any nitrogen compounds in the soil turns yellow and grows poorly. Why?

options.text_md: The nitrogen in the air is too heavy to reach the leaves.
Wheat needs oxygen gas only and does not need nitrogen.
Plants cannot use nitrogen gas directly, so it must first be changed into nitrates or ammonium compounds.
Plants take in nitrogen gas only at night.

questions.solution_md: Nitrogen gas is very unreactive and plants cannot take it up. Fixation by bacteria, or lightning, or fertiliser factories, makes compounds that roots can absorb — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A steel tumbler of cold lemonade soon has drops of water on its outside. Which step of the water cycle is the same process?

options.text_md: Evaporation of sea water
Transpiration from leaves
Condensation of water vapour into cloud droplets
Infiltration into the soil

questions.solution_md: Water vapour in the warm air touches the cold steel and turns into liquid drops. This is condensation, the same step that forms cloud droplets — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A leafy plant in a pot is covered with a transparent polythene bag and kept in the sun. After some hours drops of water appear on the inside of the bag. Which part of the water cycle does this model?

options.text_md: Infiltration followed by runoff
Transpiration followed by condensation
Precipitation followed by evaporation
Nitrification followed by respiration

questions.solution_md: The leaves lose water vapour by transpiration. The vapour cools on the bag and condenses into drops — option (b).

questions.stem_md:

**Reason (R):** Petrol is made from the remains of ancient living things that took in carbon dioxide when they were alive.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Farmers in Punjab often grow gram or moong between two wheat crops to improve the soil.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. The bacteria add nitrogen compounds to the soil, which the next crop can use, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The nitrogen cycle would work well even if all decomposers were removed.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution_md: A is false: decomposers turn nitrogen compounds in dead remains and wastes back into ammonia, so the cycle would stall without them. R is a true statement — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Wheat plants can absorb nitrogen gas straight from the air through their leaves.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.stem_md: In nitrification, soil bacteria change ammonia into ______, which plant roots can absorb.

Denitrification

Carbon dioxide is built into sugars

questions.stem_md: Name two ways in which nitrogen gas of the air is changed into compounds that plants can use.

questions.stem_md: Name two processes that take carbon dioxide out of the air and two that put it back into the air.

answer.model_answer_md: Photosynthesis by plants and algae, and the dissolving of carbon dioxide in the sea, take it out of the air. Respiration by living things, and the burning of wood and fuels, put carbon dioxide back into the air.

questions.solution_md: Out: photosynthesis, dissolving in sea. In: respiration, burning.

Two correct processes that release carbon dioxide

questions.stem_md: Describe how a drop of sea water can fall as rain on a hill in Kerala and return to the sea. Name the processes in order.

questions.stem_md: Explain the carbon cycle in the biosphere and the atmosphere. Include photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition, burning of fuels and the part played by the ocean.

answer.model_answer_md: Plants and algae take in carbon dioxide from the air and build it into sugars and wood by photosynthesis. Animals get carbon by eating plants. When plants and animals die, bacteria and fungi decompose them and release carbon dioxide, and some remains are buried and become coal, oil and gas over millions of years. questions.solution_md: Photosynthesis in; respiration, decomposition, burning out; ocean exchange.

marking_scheme.step: Photosynthesis removes carbon dioxide and builds sugars; animals eat plants
Respiration and decomposition release carbon dioxide

Ocean absorbs and releases carbon dioxide

questions.stem_md: Describe the nitrogen cycle. Explain nitrogen fixation, nitrification and denitrification, and the role of decomposers and of plants.

answer.model_answer_md: Air is about 78 percent nitrogen gas, which plants cannot use. In nitrogen fixation, bacteria such as Rhizobium in root nodules, lightning and fertiliser factories change it into ammonia or nitrates. In nitrification, soil bacteria change ammonia into nitrates. Plants absorb nitrates and make proteins, and animals get nitrogen by eating plants. Decomposers break down dead remains and wastes into ammonia. In denitrification, bacteria in waterlogged soil change nitrates back into nitrogen gas, which returns to the air.

questions.solution_md: Fixation, nitrification, uptake by plants, decomposers, denitrification.

Nitrification: ammonia to nitrates by soil bacteria

Decomposers return ammonia; denitrification returns nitrogen gas

questions.stem_md: A large forest is cleared and burned to make room for a farm. What is the effect on the carbon cycle?

Carbon dioxide is released by the burning and fewer trees remain to take it back from the air.
There is no effect, because trees do not hold carbon.
Oxygen is turned into carbon dioxide inside the soil.

questions.solution_md: The carbon stored in the trees is released as carbon dioxide when they are burned, and fewer trees are left to carry out photosynthesis — option (b).

questions.stem_md: After heavy rain, fertiliser from nearby fields washes into a lake. Soon the lake turns green with algae, and later many fish die. The most likely reason for the fish deaths is that:

options.text_md: decomposers use up the oxygen dissolved in the water as the dead algae rot
the fertiliser is a poison that kills fish at once
the algae eat the fish
the lake becomes too cold for the fish

questions.solution_md: The extra nitrogen and other nutrients make algae grow very fast. When the algae die, decomposers feed on them and use up the oxygen of the water, so the fish cannot breathe — option (a).

options.text_md: Burn crop waste in the fields and plant trees
Use more coal for power and use more fertiliser
Plant trees along the roads and generate electricity from solar panels
Cut forests for timber and use solar panels

questions.solution_md: Trees take carbon dioxide from the air, and solar panels produce power without burning fuel — option (c). The other pairs each include an action that adds carbon dioxide.

questions.stem_md: Explain why using too much fertiliser on a farm can harm a nearby river.

answer.model_answer_md: Extra fertiliser washes off the field into the river and adds nutrients to the water. This makes algae grow too much, and when the algae die, decomposers use up the oxygen, so fish and other water life may die.

questions.stem_md: Explain how human activities have changed the amount of carbon dioxide in the air and affected the climate. Suggest three actions that can reduce the problem.

answer.model_answer_md: Before the late 1800s the air held about 280 ppm of carbon dioxide. As of the early 2020s it is about 420 ppm, mainly because we burn coal, oil and gas and cut forests. Extra carbon dioxide absorbs more heat radiated by the ground, so the average temperature of the Earth has risen by about 1.1 degrees Celsius. Ice melts, sea level rises and weather becomes more extreme. We can use solar and wind power, plant trees, use public transport, and use fertiliser carefully.

questions.stem_md: Before the late 1800s the air held about 280 ppm of carbon dioxide, and as of the early 2020s it holds about 420 ppm (both approximate). By what percentage has the concentration risen?
questions.solution_md: Rise $= 420 - 280 = 140\ \text{ppm}$. Percentage rise $= \dfrac{140}{280} \times 100 = 50\%$.

The table gives the carbon dioxide concentration in the air, measured at a mountain observatory in Hawaii. The values are rounded and approximate.

| Year | Carbon dioxide (ppm) |
|---|---|
| 1960 | 317 |
| 1980 | 339 |
| 2000 | 370 |
| 2020 | 414 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) 2000 to 2020

**(b)** The rise is 97 ppm, because 414 minus 317 is 97.

**(c)** (i) Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon that was stored underground for millions of years. Cutting and burning forests releases stored carbon and reduces photosynthesis, so less carbon dioxide is removed from the air.

**OR** (ii) The claim is weak. A small amount of a greenhouse gas can absorb a lot of heat, and the rise of 97 ppm is a large increase of the carbon dioxide already in the air, nearly one third over 1960. So it does matter for climate.

questions.solution_md:

(ii) Small amounts can still strengthen the greenhouse effect.
